title: Sunitinib 37.5 mg · pancreatic NET
context_label: Progressive unresectable or metastatic well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour under NCCP 00327a.
purpose: Sunitinib is a daily targeted capsule used to help control a pancreatic NET that cannot be removed or has spread and is progressing. The team reviews control, side effects and your priorities.
schedule_summary: Take the prescribed sunitinib dose once daily continuously, at the same time, consistently with or without food. The 28-day cycle is a review period, with no planned capsule-free week.
scope_note: Progressive unresectable or metastatic well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour under NCCP 00327a.
indication_text: Progressive unresectable or metastatic well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour under NCCP 00327a.
phases_note: The written prescription and team review determine treatment; this timeline is a reference.
timeline_note: Treatment timing is shown for orientation. Symptoms can develop on any day; no symptom band predicts an individual toxicity peak.
safety_note: Follow your oncology unit’s emergency instructions. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice; do not wait for the next appointment. Call emergency services for collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or uncontrolled bleeding.
teachback: Can you explain why this is continuous daily dosing, where to record blood pressure and when painful hands/feet or diarrhoea need a call?
consent_support: Discuss the pancreatic NET indication, benefit and trial limitations, daily dosing, blood-pressure and heart risks, thyroid/glucose effects, hand-foot symptoms, bleeding, wound healing, interactions and the testing plan.
urgent_extra: Call urgently for severe diarrhoea or dehydration, bleeding, new swelling, much less urine, severe skin blistering or symptoms of low blood sugar. Chest pain, severe breathlessness, collapse, seizure or severe headache with vision changes needs emergency assessment.

agents.name: Sunitinib
agents.mechanism: Blocks several growth and blood-vessel signals
agents.explanation: Sunitinib blocks several signalling proteins involved in tumour growth and blood-vessel formation. This can slow a pancreatic NET. Effects on healthy blood vessels and other tissues help explain high blood pressure, bleeding, wound-healing problems, thyroid changes and sore hands or feet.
agents.watch: Keep blood-pressure and blood-test appointments; report bowel, skin, heart or bleeding symptoms early.
risks: High blood pressure and heart dysfunction
Painful hands and feet / skin changes
Diarrhoea, mouth soreness, fatigue and poor appetite
Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Kidney injury / protein in urine and liver abnormalities
Rare severe skin, neurological or vascular effects; impaired wound healing

passport_visit_note: Record the prescribed dose, doses taken or held, symptoms, blood tests and review dates. A stamp records care; it does not authorise the next dose.
anatomy: Thyroid changes can contribute to tiredness. Severe headache, seizure, confusion or visual change needs emergency assessment.
Report mouth soreness, eating problems or jaw pain. Discuss dental work with your team before treatment or procedures.
Blood pressure may rise without symptoms. Keep checks; new swelling or breathlessness needs advice, and chest pain needs emergency care.
Low counts can increase infection or bleeding risk. Report fever, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding; heavy bleeding is an emergency.
Liver tests may change before symptoms appear. Attend blood tests and report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or severe abdominal pain.
Diarrhoea can cause dehydration. Follow the written plan and call for persistent symptoms, dizziness or inability to drink.
Report painful redness, swelling or blisters early. Severe widespread blistering or peeling requires urgent help.
Urine protein and kidney or glucose changes may need tests. Report reduced urine, swelling, shakiness, sweating or confusion.
anatomy_note: Selected regimen-specific effects anchored to the full-body illustration. Blood, hormone and skin effects can involve more than one area. This is not a prediction or a complete side-effect list.
administration_text: The usual starting dose for this pancreatic NET schedule is 37.5 mg once daily. Follow your label, swallow whole with water and take at the same time each day consistently with or without food. If a dose is missed, do not take an additional dose; take the usual prescribed dose the next day.

phases.label: Continuous daily sunitinib
phases.detail: This is the 37.5 mg continuous pNET schedule, not a four-weeks-on/two-weeks-off schedule. Continue only as authorised by the team.

timeline.label: 28-day review
timeline.text: Counts, kidneys/liver and prescription review; BP at every attendance.

day_groups.title: Start with a clear prescription
day_groups.body: Confirm the continuous dose, blood-pressure plan, skin care and other medicines.
day_groups.action: Record any existing bowel, mouth, skin or heart symptoms.

day_groups.title: Keep taking daily unless told to hold
day_groups.body: Use the written symptom plan and report changes early. A new review window does not create a break.
day_groups.action: Attend review bloods; thyroid tests are due every 12 weeks.

support.title: Skin and mouth care
support.text: Use the unit’s gentle skin and mouth-care plan. Report hand-foot pain before it limits walking or daily tasks; the team may adjust treatment.

support.title: Sickness and diarrhoea
support.text: This oral regimen is minimal-to-low emetogenic. Routine premedication is not required. Agree rescue anti-sickness and antidiarrhoeal medicines and when to call.

support.title: Blood pressure and glucose
support.text: Follow the agreed BP plan. If you use diabetes medicines, ask how to monitor glucose and manage low readings; sunitinib may lower blood sugar.

support.title: Nutrition and fatigue
support.text: Report poor intake, weight loss or troublesome fatigue. Thyroid changes, anaemia, dehydration or other causes may need treatment.

monitoring_schedule.note: Your team books and reviews each test. Response scans and hormone or tumour markers follow an individual plan; they are not automatically required at every medicine review.

monitoring_summary: Baseline blood count, kidney/liver, thyroid and blood pressure; urine protein assessment and cardiac tests as indicated. Counts, kidney and liver tests before each cycle; BP at each attendance; thyroid every 12 weeks. Heart, urine and glucose monitoring are individualised. Scans and tumour markers follow the consultant plan.

chronology_notes.title: Continuous does not mean unchecked
chronology_notes.text: Take capsules daily only as prescribed; reviews, test results or toxicity can lead to a pause or dose change.

chronology_notes.title: No borrowed rest week
chronology_notes.text: Other sunitinib schedules use breaks. This pancreatic NET regimen is continuous; follow its own calendar.

chronology_notes.title: After a hold
chronology_notes.text: Record the last dose and reason. Your oncology team decides when and at what dose to restart.

sections.title: Capsules and missed doses

If a dose is missed, do not take an additional dose; take the usual prescribed dose the next day.

sections.title: Interactions
sections.text: Avoid grapefruit and St John’s wort. Ask the pharmacist to review every medicine and supplement, including blood thinners, antibiotics and medicines affecting heart rhythm.

sections.title: Surgery and dental work
sections.text: Tell your team about planned operations, wounds or invasive dental work. A treatment interruption may be needed for major surgery; the oncology and surgical teams agree when to stop and restart. Ask about a dental assessment.

sections.title: Storage and supply
sections.text: Keep capsules in their original labelled packaging, away from children, and follow storage instructions. Return unused medicine to the pharmacy. Bring your current prescription and medicine list to review.

sections.title: Pregnancy, feeding and fertility
sections.text: Tell the team about pregnancy, planned pregnancy or breastfeeding before treatment. Ask for the contraception and fertility plan specific to sunitinib, including how long precautions continue after stopping.

evidence.title: Evidence for this continuous pancreatic NET schedule
evidence.intro: The randomised trial compared daily sunitinib with placebo, with supportive care.
evidence.population: Adults with advanced well-differentiated pancreatic NET and documented recent progression.
evidence.interpretation: Sunitinib delayed progression compared with placebo in this population.
limitations: The trial stopped early; early survival findings require caution and do not predict one person’s lifespan.
The results apply to the pancreatic NET population and continuous dose studied, not every NET site or another sunitinib schedule.

chapters.title: Your sunitinib treatment
chapters.intro: This guide is for the continuous pancreatic NET regimen.

items.title: Why sunitinib?
items.text: Sunitinib is a daily targeted capsule used to help control a pancreatic NET that cannot be removed or has spread and is progressing. The team reviews control, side effects and your priorities.

items.title: How it works
items.text: Sunitinib blocks several signalling proteins involved in tumour growth and blood-vessel formation. This can slow a pancreatic NET. Effects on healthy blood vessels and other tissues help explain high blood pressure, bleeding, wound-healing problems, thyroid changes and sore hands or feet.

items.title: What the trial can tell us
items.text: Sunitinib delayed progression compared with placebo in this population. The trial stopped early; early survival findings require caution and do not predict one person’s lifespan. The results apply to the pancreatic NET population and continuous dose studied, not every NET site or another sunitinib schedule.

chapters.title: Understanding your particular NET
chapters.intro: Several different features help the team choose treatment.

items.title: Where it started and where it is now
items.text: A neuroendocrine tumour begins in cells with hormone-making features. Its starting organ and the places it has spread are separate parts of the diagnosis. A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour differs from pancreatic adenocarcinoma; a deposit in the liver may have come from another organ.

items.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
items.text: The pathology report describes how organised the cells look (differentiation) and their growth activity (grade). Ki-67 measures cells showing a growth-related protein in the sample. Its percentage describes that sample, not the amount of your body affected or your chance of survival.

items.title: Grade is different from stage
items.text: Stage describes extent; grade describes tumour biology. Either can vary independently. A well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumour and a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are distinct diagnoses and may need different treatments.

items.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
items.text: A functioning tumour produces a hormone syndrome. A nonfunctioning tumour can still cause problems through growth or pressure. Somatostatin receptor uptake on a scan shows a treatment target; it does not, on its own, identify a hormone syndrome.

items.title: Your diagnosis record
items.text: Ask for one diagnosis summary: starting organ, grade, differentiation, Ki-67 result if reported, sites involved, hormone syndrome and receptor-imaging result. Keep pending results clearly marked.

chapters.title: Making sense of tests and results
chapters.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and hormone tests answer different questions.

items.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
items.text: Blood counts assess oxygen-carrying cells, infection-fighting cells and platelets. Kidney and liver results help assess treatment safety. These checks are needed even when you feel well; a reassuring scan answers a different question.

items.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
items.text: CT and MRI show anatomy and tumour size. Somatostatin receptor imaging tests whether a particular receptor target is present. An FDG-PET scan measures uptake of a glucose-like tracer and is used selectively. Your team chooses the scans that can guide your care.

items.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
items.text: Selected markers may help answer a hormone or tumour question. Examples include 5-HIAA for serotonin-related symptoms, chromogranin A, or a specific pancreatic hormone. They are not a routine panel for every neuroendocrine tumour. Interpret changes with symptoms and imaging.

items.title: Preparing for a test
items.text: Use the laboratory instructions for fasting, food restrictions and any timed urine collection. Some medicines affect marker results, including acid-suppressing medicines and chromogranin A. Ask the team what to do; do not stop a prescribed medicine yourself.

items.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
items.text: Some hormone syndromes can affect heart valves, so an ultrasound of the heart may be requested. Inherited-risk assessment depends on the tumour and family history; multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is one example. An inherited-risk test and a test of tumour tissue answer different questions.

items.title: Who does what, and when?
items.text: For each test, write its name, purpose, booking date and result-review contact. Ask the team to set your next scan or marker date. A schedule for someone after surgery may not apply during your treatment.

chapters.title: Hormone symptoms and day-to-day changes
chapters.intro: A new symptom may come from the NET, treatment or another illness.

items.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
items.text: Keep a brief record of your usual bowel pattern, flushing, appetite, weight, pain and energy. Note new changes and when they started. This helps the team assess whether treatment, hormones or another problem needs attention.

items.title: Hormone-related symptoms
items.text: Hormone symptoms depend on the tumour: examples include flushing and watery diarrhoea, acid-related symptoms, or changes in blood sugar. An insulin-producing tumour can lower blood sugar. Ask which symptoms apply to you and whether you need a written rescue plan.

items.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
items.text: Hormone-control medicines have their own schedule. A pause in anticancer tablets does not automatically mean pausing those medicines. Before peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, the specialist team coordinates any interruption and restart of somatostatin analogue injections.

items.title: When a change is urgent
items.text: Follow your oncology emergency plan for sudden or severe symptoms. Collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or uncontrolled bleeding needs emergency assessment. Severe diarrhoea, persistent vomiting, dehydration, fever or sudden illness needs urgent oncology advice. Do not wait for a scan, an online answer or the next clinic visit.

items.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
items.text: Tell teams arranging an operation, anaesthetic or other procedure about a hormone-producing tumour or previous hormone crisis. Your specialist decides whether extra preparation is needed. Carry the agreed emergency instructions and current medicine list.

chapters.title: Your overall plan and choices
chapters.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment plan.

items.title: What are we trying to achieve?
items.text: Agree your treatment aim: slowing growth, reducing tumour size, controlling hormone symptoms or preserving daily function. A scan showing no growth may be a useful result even when the tumour has not shrunk.

items.title: How treatments fit together
items.text: Your plan may use different treatments at different times, including surgery, medicines, receptor-targeted radiation or treatment directed at the liver. Ask the team to mark your own sequence and who coordinates it.

items.title: Choosing between options
items.text: Ask why the proposed option fits the tumour site, grade, receptor findings, symptoms and your health. Discuss reasonable alternatives, observation when appropriate and suitable trials. Your team explains which options are available to you.

items.title: Evidence is about groups
items.text: Studies measure different outcomes, such as shrinkage, time before worsening and survival. Ask which outcome matters for your plan and how closely the study group matches your diagnosis. No study average can predict one person’s course.

items.title: Review points and shared decisions
items.text: Agree when to review the plan and what could lead to continuing, pausing or changing treatment. Include the effects on work, caring duties, travel and the activities that matter to you.

chapters.title: Eating, energy, practical help and support
chapters.intro: Supportive care can be used alongside treatment from the start.

items.title: Food, weight and digestion
items.text: Report weight loss, persistent diarrhoea, greasy stools or difficulty eating. Different causes need different treatment. Ask for a dietitian and whether reduced digestive-enzyme function needs assessment.

items.title: Fluids and safe activity
items.text: Use your personal fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea or heart or kidney disease. Adjust activity and rest to your energy. Report dizziness, breathlessness or fatigue that limits daily tasks so treatable causes can be checked.

items.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
items.text: Ask for help with mood, sleep, relationships, intimacy or caring responsibilities when you need it. Symptom and palliative-care teams can support comfort and quality of life while anticancer treatment continues.

items.title: Practical help
items.text: Ask your specialist nurse or social worker about transport, employment, finances and help at home. Tell them about caring responsibilities and ask which support organisations fit your needs.

items.title: A record that works without a phone
items.text: Keep a paper schedule, current medicine list and real contact numbers together. The handbook can be read without internet access. Use the written emergency plan whenever you need urgent help.

items.title: Questions to take to the next visit
items.text: For the next visit, choose the questions that matter most: my exact diagnosis; the aim of treatment; which tests I need and why; who explains results; when to call; and what help is available.

questions.q: Is my dose the continuous pancreatic NET schedule?
questions.a: For this NCCP pancreatic NET regimen, the standard starting schedule is 37.5 mg once daily continuously, with 28-day reviews and no planned rest week. Your own prescribed dose may differ.

questions.q: Who checks my BP and when are my 12-week thyroid tests?
questions.a: Blood pressure is checked at each attendance and thyroid tests every 12 weeks, with extra tests if indicated. Ask who will book them and where to record readings.

questions.q: What should I do about diarrhoea or painful hands and feet?
questions.a: Report these symptoms early and follow the written rescue and hold plan. Painful hands or feet can require interruption even at the first episode; the team confirms dose changes and restarting.

questions.q: Do my diabetes or blood-thinning medicines need extra monitoring?
questions.a: Ask the pharmacist to check the full medicine list. Diabetes may require closer glucose checks and changes to diabetes treatment; bleeding risks and interactions need individual review.

questions.q: What is the plan for dental work or surgery?
questions.a: Tell the oncology team before arranging procedures. Surgery, wounds and dental work may need a coordinated interruption, with restart decided by the treating teams.

questions.q: When will we review response and quality of life?
questions.a: Ask for the planned symptom, scan and treatment-review dates. There is no fixed total number of cycles; continued treatment depends on benefit, tolerability and your priorities.

monitoring_test_details.label: 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)
monitoring_test_details.timing: Only if requested for your hormone syndrome; the team sets the dates.
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Measures a breakdown product of serotonin to help assess selected neuroendocrine tumours.
monitoring_test_details.detail: Often a timed urine collection. Follow the laboratory’s food and medicine instructions.

monitoring_test_details.label: Chromogranin A
monitoring_test_details.timing: Only when the team considers it informative for your tumour.
monitoring_test_details.purpose: A selected tumour-marker result, interpreted with symptoms and scans.
monitoring_test_details.detail: Acid-suppressing medicines and other conditions can alter the result. It is not a routine test before every treatment; do not stop medicines yourself.

monitoring_test_details.label: Selected pancreatic hormones
monitoring_test_details.timing: Only for the hormone question identified by your specialist.
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Examples include gastrin, insulin or glucagon when the diagnosis or symptoms call for them.
monitoring_test_details.detail: The team names the test, preparation and review date; these are not a standard panel for every patient.
